newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Run-off draws low turnout in Serbian local polls.
newsitem.headline: Run-off draws low turnout in Serbian local polls.

text.p: Serbia held a run-off election on Sunday for municipal councils, two weeks after President Slobodan Milosevic's leftist coalition scored a resounding victory in national polls.
Initial reports indicated a low turnout, putting Milosevic's coalition -- whose supporters have disciplined voting habits -- in a strong position.
As of Sunday evening, some 30 percent of elgible voters had cast their ballots in the capital Belgrade and between 20 to 30 percent in Vojvodina province, state news agency Tanjug said.

Voter apathy was a serious setabck for the opposition coalition, which had hoped to make up for a poor result in the November 3 federal elections with local victories in Belgrade and other major towns.
"The communists (Milosevic supporters) have a disciplined voting corps who will go out and do their duty," said Vuk Draskovic, leader of the opposition Serbian Renewal Movement.
"But whether the first round will be repeated -- when half a million peole failed to vote in Belgrade -- that we shall find out soon."
The opposition, covering the political spectrum from liberal to right-wing nationalist, won 21 percent of the vote in the federal election earlier this month.
Milosevic's coalition, in its first electoral test since the end of a four-year Balkan war, won about 40 percent of the vote and a big majority in the federal parliament.
Sunday's run-off covers 5,603 city council seats in municipalities where no candidate managed to obtain a majority in the first round.
A few hours after polling stations opened, the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition issued a statement alleging abuses in Belgrade and several other districts.
The Zajedno coalition charged that the authorities prevented opposition members from taking part in some electoral boards, which supervise ballot counting and voting procedures.

In five polling stations around the central town of Lazarevac, police threw out Zajedno and nationalist Radical party members from the electoral boards and threatened to arrest them if they returned, the opposition statement said.

Three ruling coalition candidates in Smederevska Palanka were also serving as members of the electoral boards, according to the opposition, and were allegedly asking voters, "Did you come to vote for us or those traitors?"
The opposition accused Serbian authorities in the southern town of Nis of hiring bodyguards to prevent Zajedno members from joining the work of the electoral board.
The bodyguards were allegedly linked to the notorious paramilitary commander Zeljko Raznatovic, known as "Arkan", the statement said.
There was no public response to the allegations from Serbian authorities.

Even if the opposition coalition manages to win control of some city councils, analysts say real power will remain at the national level with Milosevic -- who retains tight control over the police, the state-run media and the economy.
